title: Die VOB im Einsatz bei gewerblichen Projekten - Best-Practices in der Arbeit mit Nachunternehmern
summary: Die Vergabe- und Vertragsordnung für Bauleistungen ist ein unverzichtbares Instrument im Bauwesen. Wir zeigen Best-Practices beim Einsatz von Nachunternehmern.
body_text: Überblick zur VOB: Vergabe- und Vertragsordnung für Bauleistungen Die VOB ist ein öffentliches Regelwerk, das bei der Planung, Vergabe und Durchführung von Bauleistungen für deren Vereinheitlichung Anwendung findet - und auch in der Zusammenarbeit von Bauherren, Planern, als auch ausführenden Nachunternehmern von zentraler Bedeutung ist. ‍ Hintergrund & Aufbau der VOB: Die VOB kennt man meist vor allem bei Bauaufträgen im öffentlichen Sektor, da öffentliche Auftraggeber gesetztlich verpflichtet sind, die Vergabe von Bauleistungen gemäß VOB/A durchzuführen, um Transparenz und Wettbewerb sicherzustellen. ‍ In privaten Bauverträgen kann die VOB freiwillig zur Anwendung kommen, wenn sich beide Vertragsparteien darauf einigen. Die VOB/B bietet in diesem Fall ein bewährtes Regelwerk, das die Interessen beider Seiten berücksichtigt. Die VOB besteht aus drei Teilen: VOB/A (Vergabeordnung) : Dieser Teil regelt das Verfahren zur Vergabe von Bauaufträgen. Er umfasst die Grundsätze zur öffentlichen Ausschreibung, beschränkten Ausschreibung und freihändigen Vergabe. Ziel ist es hierbei, dass der Auftraggeber möglichst viele Anbieter einlädt und am Ende der wirtschaftlichste Anbieter (keine reine Preis-Entscheidung, sondern auch Qualität) das Projekt erhält ‍ ‍ VOB/B (Allgemeine Vertragsbedingungen) : Die VOB/B enthält die allgemeinen Vertragsbedingungen für die Ausführung von Bauleistungen. Sie legt u. a. Regelungen zu Mängelansprüchen, Bauzeiten und Fristen, sowie Abnahme und Gewährleistung fest. Gemäß VOB/B wird beispielsweise die Gewährleistungsfrist von vier Jahren für den Bauherren gegenüber dem ausführenden Handwerksunternehmen festgelegt. ‍ VOB/C (Allgemeine Technische Vertragsbedingungen) : Dieser Teil beschreibt die technischen Details und Anforderungen, die in Bauverträgen vereinbart werden sollen. Die VOB/C soll insbesondere Missverständnisse hinsichtlich Qualität und Ausführungsstandards vermeiden.some text ‍ ‍ Einsatz der VOB/B bei gewerblichen Projekten mit Nachunternehmern Die VOB/B bietet klare Strukturen und Regelungen, die insbesondere auch in der Zusammenarbeit mit Nachunternehmern hilfreich sind. Wir zeigen hier einige Best-Practices: a) Klare Vertragsgestaltung: Stellen Sie sicher, dass alle wichtigen Klauseln der VOB/B in die Verträge mit den Nachunternehmern aufgenommen werden. Dies schafft eine einheitliche Grundlage und bietet einen verbindlichen Rahmen für die Ausführung und insbesondere Gewährleistung. Bedenken Sie aber, dass die VOB/B nur allgemeine Vertragsbedingungen vorgibt und es empfehlenswert ist, auch bspw. noch genauere Regelungen zur Dokumentation und Fristen festzulegen. Hier noch mehr zu dem Thema in unserem anderen Blog-Artikel zum Thema Nachunternehmervertrag [Link] b) Transparentes Baustellenmanagement Auch wenn das Engagement des Nachunternehmers noch so klein sein mag: Dokumentieren Sie Änderungen bei der Ausführung/Abweichungen vom Leistungsverzeichnis unbedingt schriftlich - und hinterlegen Sie diese beispielsweise auch auf CoCrafter. Außerdem können Sie als Ergänzung der VOB/B noch Vertragsstrafen bzw. Pönale-Regelungen für Fälle von Verzögerungen des Baufortschritts festlegen. Entscheidend hierbei sind auch regelmäßig Qualitätsprüfungen und dass die Arbeiten entsprechend VOB/C ausgeführt wurden. Hierzu könnten Sie für Ihre Bauleiter vor Ort beispielsweise auch die entsprechenden Checklisten in CoCrafter ablegen, um kollaborativ zu arbeiten. c) Kommunikation mit dem Nachunternehmer Nicht jeder Nachunternehmer kennt sich erfahrungsgemäß ausreichend gut mit der VOB aus - und insofern sollten Sie als Auftraggeber den Partner-Betrieben klar erklären, welche Regelungen bei der Zusammenarbeit zum Tragen kommen. Sinnvoll dabei ist, erneut insbesondere auf den Sicherheitseinbehalt hinzuweisen, als auch auszuprobieren mit Skonti bspw. Anreize für die pünktliche oder vorzeitige Fertigstellung zu vereinbaren. Erklären Sie den Nachunternehmern auch vor allem, wie Ihre Bauleiter mit strittigen Themen wie Mängelanzeigen, Abnahmen und Nachträgen vorgehen werden. Dies hilft oftmals stark, die Zusammenarbeit mit Nachunternehmern zu strukturieren und verbessern.

title: Inteligencia Artificial en logística 2025: de la analítica a la orquestación autónoma
summary: Descubre contenido especializado en IA, transporte y supply chain para anticiparte a los retos del sector.
body_text: En los últimos 5 años, la Inteligencia Artificial (IA) dejó de ser una promesa futurista para convertirse en una herramienta operativa diaria en logística. Sin embargo, el salto real no es pasar de hojas de excel a dashboards, sino de dashboards a orquestación completamente autónoma . Plataformas como TrackChain aplican IA nativa para tomar decisiones y ejecutarlas en tiempo real, reduciendo la latencia operativa y optimizando KPIs críticos. En mercados como México y EE. UU., donde la presión por entregas just-in-time y visibilidad total es cada vez mayor, la IA está marcando la diferencia entre liderar o quedar rezagado. El estado actual de la IA en logística El mercado global de IA aplicada a logística ya genera miles de millones de dólares y se espera que crezca fuertemente en los próximos años, impulsado por el comercio electrónico, la telemetría IoT y la presión de costos. En México, el crecimiento del comercio electrónico y la integración con el mercado estadounidense exigen optimización en tiempo real. La adopción de IA se concentra en: Ruteo dinámico: algoritmos que ajustan rutas según tráfico, clima y SLA. Visibilidad predictiva: estimaciones ETA basadas en múltiples fuentes. Gestión de excepciones: detección temprana de retrasos y respuesta automática. En EE. UU., la tendencia está en la automatización operativa : menos planners humanos tomando decisiones manuales y más agentes IA ejecutando flujos sin intervención. De dashboards a agentes inteligentes Los dashboards son útiles, pero requieren que un humano los interprete y actúe. Los agentes inteligentes eliminan ese cuello de botella: Reciben datos (GPS, TMS, ERP). ‍ Evalúan condiciones con reglas y modelos ML. ‍ Ejecutan acciones (reasignar, notificar, actualizar inventario). ‍ Aprenden de cada evento para optimizar futuras decisiones y seguir mejorando su autonomía. ‍ Esto significa que la IA no solo informa , sino actúa . ‍ Casos prácticos en primera y última milla ‍ ‍ Caso México — Distribuidor retail: Consolidación de múltiples GPS en un panel único. Un agente IA detecta retrasos >20 minutos y envía alertas automáticas por WhatsApp a operadores, reduciendo incidentes en un 40%. ‍ Caso EE. UU. — Operador cross-border: IA prioriza cargas perecederas y ajusta rutas en tiempo real según tiempos de cruce fronterizo, mejorando el OTIF en un 15%. ‍ Barreras de adopción y cómo superarlas Datos dispersos: solución → integración API-first. Resistencia operativa: solución → comunicación multicanal sin apps nuevas. Escalabilidad: solución → nube híbrida y arquitectura modular. Beneficios cuantificables Reducción de costos operativos: 10-20% en 6-12 meses. Mejora en cumplimiento de SLA: +15 a +30%. ‍ Menor latencia en decisiones: de horas a segundos.

title: Rio Carnival & Réveillon Money Guide
summary: Pay local merchants by QR code across Asia and Latin America. Connect your bank or card, skip ATM fees, and pay like a local in your own currency with Moreta.
body_text: Rio has two moments every year when the city collectively loses its mind, in the best way. Réveillon, when two million people in white pack Copacabana beach for New Year's Eve fireworks. And Carnival, when the entire city becomes a five-day street party (February 5–9 in 2027, if you're planning ahead). Both are absolutely worth the trip. Both will also quietly drain your wallet if you show up unprepared, because Rio during peak season runs on a payment system most tourists can't access and prices that double when the crowds arrive. Here's how the money side actually works, so you can spend your energy on the blocos instead of hunting for an ATM. First, Understand How Rio Pays Brazil runs on Pix. Not "increasingly uses Pix" — runs on it. The instant payment system built by the Central Bank of Brazil handles everything from beach caipirinhas to taxi rides, and during Carnival it's how the vast majority of street transactions happen. Vendors wading through a bloco crowd with a cooler of Antarctica cans aren't carrying card machines. They're carrying a laminated QR code on a lanyard. The catch: Pix was designed for people with Brazilian bank accounts, which means a CPF, which means paperwork no two-week visitor is doing. We covered the workaround in detail in our guide to using Pix in Brazil without a CPF , but the short version is that Moreta plugs directly into the Pix QR network. You scan the vendor's code, confirm in reais, and the money lands in their account like a local payment — no Brazilian bank, no CPF, no rejected foreign card. During Carnival, that's not a convenience. It's the difference between buying water in a crowd of 100,000 people and going thirsty. What Réveillon Actually Costs New Year's Eve in Rio is deceptively cheap or wildly expensive depending on how you do it. The fireworks themselves are free — you stand on Copacabana with everyone else, dressed in white, and watch fifteen minutes of the best pyrotechnics on the planet. The spending around it is where budgets go sideways: Beach kiosk dinner and drinks: R$150–300 per person on the night itself, roughly double normal prices Hotel parties and rooftop events: R$500–2,500+ per ticket for the big ones along Avenida Atlântica Beer or água de coco from a walking vendor: R$10–20, Pix or cash only Getting home: rideshares surge hard after midnight; expect 3–4x pricing or a very long walk One thing veterans know: the metro runs extended hours on Réveillon and is by far the sanest way in and out of Copacabana. Load a transit card in advance, because the station queues after the fireworks are brutal. What Carnival Actually Costs Carnival splits into two very different price categories. The street Carnival is nearly free. The blocos — roving street parties, hundreds of them across the city — cost nothing to join. Your spending is drinks, food and costumes, almost all of it from informal vendors. Budget R$100–200 a day if you're doing blocos, and expect nearly every transaction to be Pix or small cash. The Sambadrome is the splurge. Tickets for the main parade nights run from around R$350 for upper grandstand seats to several thousand reais for front boxes, and prices climb as the date approaches. Buy from the official channels early — the resale market around the stadium on parade night is a scam minefield. A realistic mid-range budget for five days of Carnival, including one Sambadrome night, decent food and a lot of street beer: R$2,500–4,000 per person, not counting accommodation. Speaking of which — book that now. Seriously. Rio accommodation for Carnival 2027 and Réveillon 2026/27 sells out months ahead and triples in price. Why Cash Is a Bad Plan for Both The traditional tourist approach — pull a stack of reais from an ATM and carry it around — fails in Rio's peak season for three specific reasons. ATMs run dry. During Carnival week, machines in Copacabana, Ipanema and Lapa get emptied faster than they're refilled. Finding a working ATM on the Saturday of Carnival is a genuine quest. The fees are ugly. Between the local bank's withdrawal fee (often R$25–30 per pull), your home bank's international fee and the conversion markup, you're losing 5–7% before you've bought a single beer. Crowds and cash don't mix. Rio is safer than its reputation, but pickpocketing in dense bloco crowds is real. Locals go out with a phone in a waterproof pouch and R$50 in a shoe. The less physical money you carry, the less you can lose. This is exactly why Brazilians themselves switched to QR payments for street events — a phone you're already holding is the safest wallet in a crowd. The Setup That Works Here's the pre-trip checklist that takes fifteen minutes and saves you the entire headache: Download Moreta from the App Store or Google Play and verify with your passport before you fly. Top up in your home currency while you're still on home WiFi. Airport connections and crowd-jammed networks are not where you want to be doing bank transfers. Load enough for the big days. Réveillon night and the peak Carnival weekend are when you'll be scanning constantly — water, beer, food, more water. Keep R$100–150 in small notes as backup for the rare vendor who hasn't caught up, and for tipping. Check the recipient name after every scan. Pix shows you who you're paying before you confirm. Locals glance at it every time, especially in busy crowds. Do the same. The rate you see in the app before confirming is the rate you pay — a flat 1.5% on QR transactions, no dynamic currency conversion games, no surprise on your statement in January. A Few Crowd-Tested Tips Buy your bloco drinks from the vendors with coolers, not the bars. They're cheaper, faster, and they all take Pix. The guy selling ice-cold cans out of a styrofoam box is the true infrastructure of Carnival. Phone battery is money. If your phone dies, so does your wallet. A small power bank is the single most valuable thing you'll carry during a twelve-hour bloco day. Screenshot your accommodation address and keep a little cash for a taxi in case your phone does die at 4am in Lapa. Redundancy is not paranoia during Carnival. Agree on prices before handing anything over. Costume pieces, chair rentals on the beach, "helpful" parking guys — peak season brings peak creativity in pricing. A friendly "quanto custa?" first solves most of it. One Wallet, Whole Trip Plenty of travelers pair Rio with the rest of the continent — Buenos Aires after Carnival, or Peru before it. The same Moreta wallet that scans Pix codes in Rio handles MODO in Argentina and Yape in Peru, and if your travels swing the other direction, PromptPay in Thailand and beyond. One balance, one app, every QR code on the route. Réveillon and Carnival are two of the best parties on Earth, and the people throwing them stopped carrying cash years ago. Set yourself up before you fly, and you can stop thinking about money roughly thirty seconds after you land. If anything gets weird mid-bloco, the Help Center has you covered — and yes, someone actually answers.

title: How to Fly First Class with Points
summary: First class books from around 85,000 points for a suite that sells for $12,000 or more. See which programs open it, what it costs, and how to book it.
body_text: How to Fly First Class with Points A first-class suite from New York to Tokyo sells for $12,000 to $20,000 in cash. The same seat can book from around 85,000 credit card points. That is not a typo. Flying first class with points is the single most dramatic value in travel, and it is not reserved for the wealthy or for people who fly for work. Here is the value gap. Redeem your points through a credit card portal and they are worth about 1 to 1.5 cents each ( CFPB ). Transfer them to the right airline and they can be worth 2 to 20 times that. First class sits at the top of that range, the full 20x, because the cash fares are so high. First class is also the hardest award to find. The cabins are tiny, seats are released unpredictably, and some airlines open first class only to their own members. This guide is honest about both sides, because the value is real and so is the scarcity. You will learn which programs open first class to everyday points holders, what it costs in points versus cash, why the space is so hard to find, and how to catch and book it. At Pointhound, we track award availability across 200+ airlines and 21 loyalty programs on 75,000+ routes, so you can see which first-class seats your points can book before you transfer anything. First Class vs Business Class with Points: What You Get and What It Costs First class costs more points than business, often 1.5 to 3 times as much on the same route, but it delivers a private suite instead of a lie-flat seat and the widest cash-to-points gap in travel. The cabin difference is real, not marketing. Business class means a lie-flat seat that turns into a bed, usually in a pod with some privacy. First class means an enclosed private suite, and on the top products a separate bed, a closing door, standalone dining, or even a shower in the sky on the Emirates A380. First class exists on far fewer aircraft and routes, which is part of why the seats are so scarce. The point cost climbs with the cabin. A business class award to Asia runs roughly 60,000 to 115,000 points one-way. First class on the same kind of route runs roughly 80,000 to 160,000. You pay more points, but the cash price you are replacing jumps even faster, which is why first class has the best cents-per-point value of any redemption when you can find it. Cabin Typical points (one-way) Typical cash (one-way) Availability Business class 60,000 to 115,000 $3,000 to $8,000 Widely released across many programs First class 80,000 to 186,000 $10,000 to $25,000 Scarce, few programs, few seats One honest recommendation: if this is your first premium redemption, start with business class. It is cheaper in points, far easier to find, and still a lie-flat seat across an ocean. Our guide on how to find cheap business class flights with points covers that playbook in full. Treat first class as the reach goal, not the starting point. Which Programs Actually Open First Class to Transferable Points? A handful of programs open first class to holders of transferable points: Singapore KrisFlyer, Virgin Atlantic for ANA, Cathay Pacific Asia Miles, American AAdvantage for Japan Airlines, and Emirates Skywards. Each is reachable from a different set of cards. The program you book through matters more than the airline you fly. Here is where the value lives, with the lowest realistic point costs and the honest limitation for each. Singapore Airlines first class, through KrisFlyer. Singapore keeps its lowest-priced first class and Suites awards for its own KrisFlyer members and does not release them to partner airlines ( The Points Guy ). The upside for beginners is huge: all five transferable programs feed KrisFlyer, so whatever points you hold, you can reach it. First class runs from around 132,500 miles one-way on routes like Los Angeles to Tokyo. The catch: the famous A380 Suites do not fly to the United States, so US departures use aircraft without a first cabin. ANA first class, through Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. ANA runs one of the best first-class cabins in the sky, and it books from around 85,000 Virgin points one-way, less from the West Coast, for a seat that sells for $10,000 to $15,000 ( NerdWallet ). Virgin Atlantic takes transfers from all five major programs. One quirk: ANA awards through Virgin have to be booked by phone, and ANA releases few first-class seats, often only close to departure. Japan Airlines first class, through American AAdvantage. This is the low-fee standout. Japan Airlines first books for about 80,000 AAdvantage miles one-way plus roughly $5.60 in taxes ( The Points Guy ), for a cabin that sells above $12,000. The limit is access: among the five transferable programs, Bilt is the one that feeds AAdvantage at 1:1 (Marriott transfers at 3:1). If you hold only Chase or Amex points, this one is out of direct reach. Cathay Pacific first class, through Asia Miles. Cathay first runs about 125,000 miles one-way from Los Angeles and 160,000 from New York ( The Points Guy ), for a seat that sells above $12,000. Asia Miles takes transfers from Amex (at a 5:4 ratio), Capital One, Citi, and Bilt. Just know that Cathay releases little first-class space to partner programs, so open seats are rare. Emirates first class, through Emirates Skywards. Emirates first, with the onboard shower and lounge, runs about 163,500 to 186,000 Skywards miles one-way from the US to Dubai, plus roughly $800 to $900 in carrier surcharges ( One Mile at a Time ). Bilt transfers to Skywards at 1:1, Amex and Citi at 5:4, and Capital One at a reduced ratio as of January 2026 ( Emirates ). The catch is a big one: Emirates now requires Skywards elite status to book first class with its own miles, and the surcharges are steep, so this is not a beginner-friendly pick. Book through First class you fly From (one-way) Cash range Cards that feed it Singapore KrisFlyer Singapore first class 132,500 miles $18,000 to $25,000 Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, Bilt Virgin Atlantic Flying Club ANA first class 85,000 points $10,000 to $15,000 Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, Bilt American AAdvantage Japan Airlines first class 80,000 miles + $5.60 $10,000 to $15,000 Bilt (Marriott at 3:1) Cathay Asia Miles Cathay first class 125,000 miles $12,000 to $21,000 Amex, Capital One, Citi, Bilt Emirates Skywards Emirates first class 163,500 miles + $800 $8,000 to $17,000 Bilt, Amex, Capital One, Citi What First Class Actually Costs in Points vs Cash First-class awards run from roughly 80,000 to 186,000 points one-way, for seats that sell for $10,000 to $25,000 in cash. That is the widest cash-to-points gap of any redemption you can make. The math is what makes people do a double-take. A $12,000 seat for 80,000 points works out to about 15 cents per point, roughly ten times what the same points return through a card portal. That is the 20x end of the transfer-value range made concrete. First-class product Cash (one-way) Points (one-way) Value per point Japan Airlines, via AAdvantage ~$12,000 80,000 + $5.60 ~15 cents ANA, via Virgin Atlantic ~$12,000 85,000 ~14 cents Cathay Pacific, via Asia Miles ~$15,000 125,000 ~12 cents Two honest notes before you get carried away. First, the point cost is high in absolute terms, and one welcome bonus often is not enough for a round-trip first-class ticket. Second, surcharges vary widely: Japan Airlines charges about $5.60 in fees, while Emirates can add $900. Always check the full cash-plus-points total, not just the miles. One upside worth knowing: award bookings can sometimes earn miles, depending on the program, so a points ticket is not always a dead end. If the portal-versus-transfer idea is new to you, our guide on credit card portal vs transferring points explains why the same points are worth so much more through an airline. And for the routes where points stretch furthest, see where your points go furthest . Why First-Class Award Space Is So Hard to Find First-class award space is scarce because airlines release few first seats as awards, some open them only to their own members, and the rules change without notice. There are three reasons the seats are so hard to catch. The cabins are tiny to begin with, sometimes only eight seats on the whole plane, so there is little to release. Some programs never share first class with partners, like Singapore, or open it only close to departure, like ANA. And the rules shift under your feet. Lufthansa is the cautionary tale. For years, its first-class award space opened to partner programs like Air Canada Aeroplan close to departure, a well-known way to book that cabin. Then, as of June 1, 2026, Lufthansa stopped releasing first-class award space to partner programs entirely ( One Mile at a Time ). A path that worked last year can vanish this year. That is why you never assume a route is bookable and never transfer points on speculation. Some of this scarcity is a timing problem: a few programs release premium space in a second wave close to takeoff. That is a whole strategy on its own, and we cover it in last-minute award flights . The short version is that a search across many programs at once beats refreshing airline sites by hand, which is exactly what a tool that scans 21 loyalty programs is for. How to Find and Book a First-Class Award, Step by Step To book first class with points, search live availability first, match the seat to the cheapest program you can reach, confirm it is bookable, transfer the exact points, then book directly with the airline. Step 1: Know your points and their reach before you start. Tally your balances across Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt, and know which first-class programs each one can reach. Amex gets you to ANA, Singapore, and Cathay. Bilt is your path to Japan Airlines first. New to award travel? Our guide on how to book flights with credit card points covers the basics. Step 2: Search live first-class availability across programs. First seats are rare, so checking airline by airline wastes the small window you have. Pointhound searches 21 loyalty programs and 200+ airlines at once and shows which program books each seat, at what cost, with step-by-step instructions. Pointhound is a search-and-discovery tool, not a booking site, so you complete the booking with the airline. Step 3: Confirm the seat is bookable before you transfer. This is the rule that saves first-class trips. Most transfers are instant, but some Amex partners take up to five days, and points cannot move back out of an airline program once they land. Verify the exact award is live first, then transfer. Step 4: Transfer the exact number of points, then book immediately. First-class awards are often a single seat, and they disappear fast. Move only what the booking needs and complete it the moment the points arrive. Hesitate and someone else takes the suite. Step 5: Let alerts catch the rare release. Because first-class space opens unpredictably, Pointhound Flight Alerts track 70,000+ routes and send an SMS or email the moment a first seat opens on a route you are watching. If you would rather have deals come to you, Pointhound's Deal Discovery emails match curated award releases to your programs and home airports, with all-cabin deals for Premium subscribers. The order never changes: search first, transfer last. That single habit is what separates a booked first-class seat from points stranded in a program with nothing to spend them on. Frequently Asked Questions Can you really fly first class with credit card points? Yes. A handful of programs, including Singapore KrisFlyer, Virgin Atlantic for ANA, Cathay Asia Miles, American AAdvantage for Japan Airlines, and Emirates Skywards, book international first class, and all take transfers from major credit card programs. The space is limited, but it is real and repeatable. How many points do you need for a first-class flight? Roughly 80,000 to 186,000 points one-way, depending on the airline and route. Japan Airlines first runs about 80,000 AAdvantage miles, ANA first about 85,000 Virgin points, Cathay first 125,000 to 160,000 Asia Miles, and Emirates first 163,500 or more Skywards miles plus surcharges. Is first class worth the extra points over business class? Sometimes. First class costs 1.5 to 3 times the points of business on the same route, for a private suite instead of a lie-flat seat. The value per point can still be excellent because first-class cash fares are so high, but business class is the better everyday value for most travelers. Which credit card points are best for first class? It depends on the airline. Amex reaches ANA, Singapore, and Cathay. Capital One and Citi reach several first-class programs. Bilt is the transferable program that feeds American AAdvantage for Japan Airlines first, and it also transfers 1:1 to Emirates Skywards, which makes it unusually useful for premium cabins. Why can't I find first-class award seats? First-class cabins are tiny, some airlines never release first to partners or open it only near departure, and the rules change. Lufthansa stopped sharing first-class awards with partner programs in mid-2026. Search live availability instead of assuming, and set an alert to catch a release. Key Takeaways Flying first class with points is the single most dramatic value in travel: a $12,000 to $25,000 suite from roughly 85,000 points, the 20x end of the transfer-value range. First class costs 1.5 to 3 times the points of business class on the same route, for a private suite instead of a lie-flat seat. The programs that open first class to transferable points are Singapore KrisFlyer, Virgin Atlantic for ANA, Cathay Asia Miles, American AAdvantage for Japan Airlines, and Emirates Skywards. Japan Airlines first is the low-fee standout at about 80,000 miles plus $5.60; Emirates first carries roughly $900 in surcharges and now needs Skywards status. First-class space is genuinely scarce and the rules change, as Lufthansa's mid-2026 partner-award closure showed. Never assume, always search live. Confirm the seat before transferring, and set Flight Alerts to catch the rare release. What to Do Next First class is not a fantasy reserved for the rich. It is reachable with points you may already hold, if you know which programs open it and you are willing to be flexible and quick when a seat appears. The trade-off is real: the space is scarce and the rules move. The reward is a $15,000 suite for a fraction of the cash. Start by searching live first-class availability on Pointhound for free. Set a Flight Alert on your target route so the rare seat finds you instead of the other way around. And if you are new to using points for flights, begin with our guide on how to book flights with credit card points . Sources Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. title: What does CARE Certified mean?
summary: In an era where consumers are increasingly concerned about the ethics and stories behind their food choices, the CARE Certified program stands out as a comprehensive certification.CARE Certified is a sustainability standard that verifies: • Animal welfare • Environmental stewardship • Community impact By having three specific pillars, it provides a holistic approach to responsible food production.Love for Our Animals | Farmers and Rancher Raising Animals with Love and CAREWhat Does CARE Certif
body_text: In an era where consumers are increasingly concerned about the ethics and stories behind their food choices, the CARE Certified program stands out as a comprehensive certification. CARE Certified is a sustainability standard that verifies: Animal welfare Environmental stewardship Community impact By having three specific pillars, it provides a holistic approach to responsible food production. What Does CARE Certified Mean? CARE Certified is a sustainability standard that signifies a commitment to humane animal care practices, environmental responsibility, and community well-being. For farmers and ranchers raising your food, this certification indicates that their operations adhere to rigorous standards designed to ensure the health and welfare of animals, land, and the community. CARE Certified for Beef As of today, the program includes: 1,200+ ranches 33 states Over 1.1 million certified animals It ensures animals are raised with attention to welfare, handling, and overall care. The certification aims to provide consumers with verified humane beef options, helping them make informed choices aligned with their values. What Expectations Are Included in CARE Certified? The CARE Certified program encompasses a set of robust requirements designed to ensure the humane treatment of animals. Some key components of the Animal Care pillar include: Handler / Employee Training Antibiotic Stewardship Safe Transportation Animal Identification Secure Supply Chain Procedures/Processes Animal Health and Nutrition Plan Allow Cattle to Express Natural Behaviors Some key components of the Environmental Stewardship pillar include: Land and Water Resources Grazing Management Plan Animal Productivity Waste Management Energy Reduction Long-term Strategy Some key components of the People & Community pillar include: Safe Working Environment Employee Growth and Development Opportunities Legacy and Succession Planning Local Community Support How CARE Certified Is Verified Verification to the CARE Certified standard involves a thorough process designed to ensure compliance with the established requirements. This includes: Initial Assessment Producers undergo an initial assessment to evaluate their animal care practices against the CARE Certification standards. Annual on-Farm Audits Annual on-farm audits are conducted to verify adherence to standards. These audits assess various aspects of animal welfare, environmental stewardship, and people and community-focused practices. Documentation Review Producers are required to maintain comprehensive records that demonstrate compliance with the animal care standards. These documents and records are reviewed by on-site auditors and reviewers to ensure they meet the standards. Corrective Actions If any deficiencies are identified during audits, producers must implement corrective actions to address the issues and improve their practices. Ongoing Annual Review Annual reviews ensure that standards are maintained, and necessary adjustments are made to uphold the integrity of the CARE Certified label and the standard itself. Who Verifies CARE Certified? CARE Certified is verified onsite by independent third-party auditors and internal reviewers who specialize in animal welfare and sustainability standards. These auditors and reviewers assess compliance with the CARE Certification requirements through on-site visits and comprehensive evaluations that are aligned in the CARE Certified Standard. Why It Stands Out While many animal welfare programs exist, CARE Certified distinguishes itself by integrating animal care with environmental stewardship and community impact. This holistic approach ensures that all aspects of sustainability are addressed. Compared to other certifications, CARE Certified emphasizes: Comprehensive Standards: CARE Certified includes criteria for animal welfare, environmental stewardship practices, and community engagement, making it a well-rounded sustainability standard. Transparency, Traceability and Verification: The rigorous verification process ensures that claims are substantiated via traceability and verification, providing consumers with confidence in the products they purchase. Educational Focus: CARE Certified encourages ongoing education and training for producers, fostering a culture of continuous improvement in animal welfare practices, as well as environmental and community and people support. Why Brands and Producers Use CARE Certified Brands and producers choose to pursue CARE Certified for several reasons: Commitment to Sustainability: For producers, obtaining CARE Certified status reflects a genuine commitment to animal welfare, environmental stewardship, and community well-being, enhancing their reputation and credibility. They understand that many consumers today are very disconnected from the food they eat. They want to be able to share their story and their commitment to sustainability and providing a safe, nutritious product and participating in a program like CARE Certified allows that to be communicated through the CARE Certified label on food products. Consumer Demand: As consumers become more conscious of their food choices, brands that offer CARE Certified products can meet the growing demand for ethically and sustainably produced beef, pork, poultry and dairy products. Market Differentiation: The CARE Certified label sets products apart in a competitive marketplace, allowing brands to appeal to socially responsible consumers. Common Questions About CARE Certified Is it regulated? Yes, CARE Certified operates under strict standards that are regularly reviewed and updated. A committee of experts in the focus areas of CARE also review the standards on an annual basis. The certification process ensures that producers adhere to established guidelines for animal welfare, environmental stewardship, and people and community. There are also traceability measures that must be in place to be approved as well, ensure complete supply-chain traceability of animals and products. Is it audited annually? Yes, CARE Certified producers participate in annual audits to ensure ongoing compliance with the certification standards and to continuously improve their practices. This helps maintain the integrity of the certification. What does it help promote? CARE Certified promotes the farms, brands and retailers that prioritize humane treatment of animals, adhere to environmental stewardship practices, and engage positively with their communities. It assures consumers that they are supporting ethical and sustainable food production. Bottom Line CARE Certified is more than just a label; it represents a commitment to animal welfare, environmental sustainability, and community responsibility. By choosing CARE Certified, consumers can feel confident that they are supporting ethical practices that prioritize the well-being of animals and the environment. As awareness and demand for humane treatment of livestock continue s to grow, programs like CARE Certified play a crucial role in shaping the future of sustainable agriculture.

body_text: View all news The Trade Desk Appoints Vinny Rinaldi as Vice President of Client Strategy & Growth July 16, 2026 Download (opens in new window) Industry veteran brings decades of marketing, data and digital transformation experience to help brands maximize business outcomes in the AI era VENTURA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- The Trade Desk, a leading advertising technology company, today announced that Vinny Rinaldi has joined the company as Vice President of Client Strategy & Growth. In this role, Rinaldi will partner closely with marketers to help them unlock greater value from data-driven advertising, navigate the rapidly evolving media landscape and accelerate business growth through the premium open internet. Rinaldi will report to Chief Operating Officer, Vivek Kundra. Rinaldi joins The Trade Desk with more than two decades of experience leading marketing transformation initiatives for some of the world's most recognizable brands. Most recently, Vinny served as Vice President of Consumer Connections at The Hershey Company. Prior to that, he’s worked on both agency and technology side, with stints at Amazon, Google, GroupM and Dentsu. Throughout his career, he has helped organizations modernize their marketing capabilities, connect data and technology investments to measurable business outcomes, and build customer-centric strategies that drive long-term growth. "The future of advertising belongs to marketers who can combine data, technology and human expertise to make smarter decisions," said Jeff Green, CEO and Co-Founder of The Trade Desk. "Vinny understands what it takes to help brands transform themselves for that future. He brings a unique combination of strategic vision, marketing expertise and customer focus that will help our clients thrive as AI reshapes our industry." At The Trade Desk, Rinaldi will work with brands and agency partners to develop growth strategies that leverage the company's industry-leading technology, data-driven decisioning capabilities and premium open internet inventory. He will also advise customers on emerging opportunities across connected TV, retail media, digital audio and other high-growth channels as AI continues to reshape advertising. "The advertising industry is entering a new era where marketers have unprecedented opportunities to make every advertising dollar work harder," said Rinaldi. "The Trade Desk has consistently led the industry by giving marketers more transparency, more control and better performance. I'm excited to join the team and help customers harness data, technology and AI to achieve stronger business outcomes." Rinaldi's appointment reflects The Trade Desk's continued investment in helping marketers navigate an increasingly dynamic advertising ecosystem while driving measurable growth through objective, data-driven media buying. He starts on July 27th. His hire follows the recent appointments of Nate Olmstead as Chief Financial Officer, Sarah Gavin as Chief Marketing Officer, Executive Vice President and Kristi Argyilan as Chief Commercial Officer, Executive Vice President, further strengthening The Trade Desk's leadership team as the company enters its next phase of growth. About The Trade Desk The Trade Desk™ is a technology company that empowers buyers of advertising. Through its self-service, cloud-based platform, ad buyers can create, manage, and optimize digital advertising campaigns across ad formats and devices. Integrations with major data, inventory, and publisher partners ensure maximum reach and decisioning capabilities, and enterprise APIs enable custom development on top of the platform. Headquartered in Ventura, CA, The Trade Desk has offices across North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific. To learn more, visit thetradedesk.com or follow us on Facebook , X , LinkedIn , and YouTube . title: Lear to Participate in Wolfe Research Autos and Mobility Conference
body_text: SOUTHFIELD, Mich., June 5, 2026 -- Lear Corporation (NYSE: LEA), a global automotive technology leader in Seating and E-Systems, will participate in a fireside chat on June 18, 2026, at the Wolfe Research Autos and Mobility Conference in New York. Building on more than 100 years of heritage, Lear is the largest U.S.-based automotive supplier, headquartered in Southfield, Michigan. Driven by a commitment to innovation, operational excellence, and sustainability, Lear’s global team of talented employees is shaping the future of mobility by developing solutions that enhance comfort, safety, and efficiency. More information is available at Lear.com.

title: Final Parking Space: 1974 Jeep CJ-5
summary: While I have no problem finding discarded examples of the International Harvester Scout in the car graveyards along the I-25 corridor between Cheyenne, Wyoming, and Albuquerque, New Mexico, the Jeep CJ is a much different story. body_text: While I have no problem finding discarded examples of the International Harvester Scout in the car graveyards along the I-25 corridor between Cheyenne, Wyoming, and Albuquerque, New Mexico, the Jeep CJ is a much different story. Here’s one that now sits in its final parking space in a yard just south of Denver . Murilee Martin Before today’s FPS subject, I had documented exactly one Jeep CJ in a self-service wrecking yard: this ’74 that I found near Denver back in 2024 . Murilee Martin In fact, before today’s Jeep, I had written about more junked Austin Champs than I had about junked CJs. These right-hand-drive British soldiers and their Rolls-Royce engines (seen above) ended their careers in the Centennial State. Murilee Martin It is possible to find the CJ-5’s rear-wheel-drive DJ-5 Dispatcher cousin in the Ewe Pullets of the land, because the US Postal Service bought so many of them during the 1969–1984 period, and it’s a major job to convert one to four-wheel-drive and then move the steering wheel to the left side. Murilee Martin If you’re looking for the simplest possible motor vehicle, essentially a steel box on wheels with an automatic transmission bolted to whatever engine Kaiser or AMC was able to source for the least money when built, the USPS DJ-5 is your car… but most examples don’t hold their value enough to avoid a junkyardy fate when they get worn out. I’ve documented many DJ-5s during my boneyard travels. Aaron McKenzie The CJ-5 has held its value in recent decades, and that means that rough ones nearly always get rescued before they end up in the crusher’s cold steel jaws . If nothing else, they get stashed away as parts donors for restoration projects. Stellantis The CJ-5 was built from 1954 through 1983 and was at heart a civilianized version of the Korean War–era Willys M38A1 . It wasn’t comfortable, but it was better suited for everyday street driving than its CJ-3 predecessor , which stayed in production into the late 1960s. Murilee Martin If you were doing your vehicle shopping in Japan, you could buy a new Mitsubishi-built CJ-3 ( called the J3 ) all the way through the late 1990s. The global Jeep CJ production story has too many plot twists to cover here, but it’s worth noting that Mahindra built CJ-3s in India until 2010. Murilee Martin The direct ancestor of all the CJs was the original Jeep, the Willys MB of World War II fame. Here’s a street-driven ’44 GPW (the Ford-built version) in the parking lot of the Bastogne War Museum in Belgium . American Motors Corporation The CJ-5 was a narrow vehicle, which made it tippy but also capable of squeezing past obstacles on difficult trails. Unlike its military cousins, it had some comfort and convenience features and was designed to tolerate sustained pavement driving. Murilee Martin The CJ-5 was designed by Willys and went into production soon after that company was purchased by Kaiser Motors. The American Motors Corporation bought Kaiser-Jeep in 1970 and continued CJ-5 production through the end. Murilee Martin The CJ-5 became a much more street-capable machine during the AMC era. The wheelbase got a 2½-inch stretch for 1972, and beefy Kenosha engines replaced the ancient Willys Hurricane F-head inline-four and Buick 225-cubic-inch V-6 . Murilee Martin The base engine for the early AMC-era CJ-5 was the 232-cubic-inch pushrod straight-six, with the 258-cubic-inch six and 304-cubic-inch V-8 as optional equipment. This truck has the 258, which was rated at 110 horsepower and 185 pound-feet for 1974. This was good power for a vehicle that scaled in at just 2540 pounds (its stretched CJ-6 big brother weighed 2600 pounds and had the same engine choices). Murilee Martin The build tag on the dash tells us that this CJ-5 was built at the plant in Toledo, Ohio , during July of 1974. Murilee Martin The transmission is the base three-speed manual. Four-speed manuals and three-speed automatics were available as options in 1974. Murilee Martin Air conditioning wasn’t available in the CJ-5 until 1977, but this luxurious heater/defroster/vent system was standard equipment for 1974. Murilee Martin Various soft- and hard-cab and roof options were available from the factory, but this truck has an obvious aftermarket steel body added. Murilee Martin This is a Koenig Iron Works Model 550 hardtop rig , built in Houston. The pre-ZIP code address on this tag suggests that it is a unit made before 1963 . Murilee Martin That explains the fact that the edge of the door hinge covers up the Jeep badge, since the AMC-era CJ-5 was longer than the Kaiser-era version. That rust hole below the door indicates scary corrosion problems that likely spelled doom for this Jeep. Murilee Martin This Koenig Iron Works window regulator design is a marvel of simplicity. Murilee Martin Do you really need more gauges than this? Murilee Martin This bolt-in roll bar looks like it’s the “racing style” factory option , but it could also be aftermarket. Murilee Martin This was a very competent off-road vehicle, but the comfort level was punitive by the SUV standards of even a decade later. Murilee Martin Judging by the large amount of rodent poop inside, it sat outdoors for a lengthy period before coming here. I’m even more careful about hantavirus than I used to be, since a Colorado friend nearly died of it recently (he believes he caught it while tearing out the interior of an old RV). Murilee Martin This truck would have had an MSRP of $3574 when new, plus the 54 extra bucks for the 258 engine. That comes to about $26,091 after inflation . That’s quite a bit more than a new Wrangler , which starts at $36,035, but that truck is like an intergalactic luxury spacecraft next to a mid-1970s CJ. “Whatcha doin’ on yer day off?” It’s noteworthy that there’s exactly zero pavement driving depicted in this commercial. “It’s got guts. Rugged Jeep guts.” Even a decade later, the ride of the CJ was pitched as comparable to a high-speed jaunt on the back of a rampaging buffalo.
